entry: American writer, musician, and [[Satanism|Satanist]]. He founded the Church of Satan in [[San Francisco]] in 1966 and developed LaVeyan Satanism, which treats Satan as a symbol of human carnality rather than a literal deity. His book *The Satanic Bible* (1969) codified its principles. He also released three albums and served as technical advisor on the film *The Devil's Rain* (1975). Historian Gareth J. Medway described him as a "born showman," but journalist Lawrence Wright found no evidence for LaVey's claim to have worked in a circus as a teenager.

Czech composer. His music draws on the rhythms of [[Folk music|folk music]] from Moravia and his native [[Bohemia]], following the nationalist example of his predecessor Bedřich Smetana. In 1877 [[Johannes Brahms|Brahms]] recommended him to his publisher, who commissioned the *Slavonic Dances*, Op. 46, which brought him international success. A [[London]] performance of his *Stabat Mater* in 1883 led to many performances in the United Kingdom and the United States. In 1892 he became director of the National Conservatory of Music of America in New York City, where he wrote the [[Symphony|Symphony]] *From the New World* and his Cello Concerto. In Spillville, Iowa, in 1893 he wrote the *American* String Quartet, among his best-known [[Chamber music|chamber music]]. He returned to Bohemia in 1895. Of his ten [[Opera|operas]], all but the first have Czech librettos, and *Rusalka* (1901) is the most successful.

Spanish architect and designer, widely described as the greatest exponent of Catalan Modernisme, a regional variant of [[Art Nouveau]]. His organic forms, inspired by natural shapes, combined ceramics, stained glass, ironwork forging, and carpentry. He introduced trencadís, a [[Mosaic|mosaic]] technique using waste ceramic pieces. Most of his works are in [[Barcelona]], including the still-incomplete [[Sagrada Família]], his magnum opus and the most-visited monument in Spain. He rarely drew detailed plans, preferring three-dimensional [[Scale model|scale models]] and shaping details as he conceived them. Between 1984 and 2005, seven of his works were declared [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Sites. His Catholic faith intensified over his life, and religious imagery appears in many works, earning him the nickname "God's Architect." [[Pope Francis]] authorized his declaration as Venerable in April 2025.

Dutch microbiologist and microscopist, active during the [[Dutch Golden Age]]. Largely self-taught, he is commonly known as the "Father of [[Microbiology]]." A draper and municipal official in Delft, he developed an interest in lensmaking and from the 1670s used [[Microscope|single-lens microscopes]] of his own design. He was the first to observe and experiment with [[Microorganism|microbes]], which he originally called *dierkens*, *diertgens*, or *diertjes*, and he was the first to estimate their size. He also documented microscopic observations of muscle fibers, [[Bacteria|bacteria]], spermatozoa, [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]], and crystals in gouty tophi, and was among the first to see blood flow in capillaries. He wrote no books; instead he described his discoveries in letters to the Royal Society, which published many of them in its *Philosophical Transactions*.

[[Spain|Spanish]] actor. Born in [[Málaga]], he made his film debut in Pedro Almodóvar's *Labyrinth of Passion* (1982), and the two went on to collaborate on eight films, including *Matador* (1986) and *Pain and Glory* (2019), for which he won the Cannes Film Festival Award for Best Actor. His Hollywood roles include *Philadelphia* (1993) with [[Tom Hanks]] and *Evita* (1996) with [[Madonna]]. He voiced Puss in Boots in the *Shrek* films and played Zorro in *The Mask of Zorro* (1998). He also directed the comedy *Crazy in Alabama* (1999).

Italian [[Marxism|Marxist]] philosopher, journalist, and politician. A founding member and one-time leader of the Italian Communist Party, he was a vocal critic of [[Benito Mussolini]] and [[Fascism]] and was imprisoned in 1926. During his imprisonment he wrote more than 30 notebooks and 3,000 pages of history and analysis, known as the *Prison Notebooks*, which are considered a highly original contribution to 20th-century political theory. Gramsci is best known for his theory of cultural hegemony, by which the state and the ruling [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeoisie]] maintain power through cultural institutions. In his view, hegemony operates through ideology rather than violence, economic force, or coercion. He sought to break from the economic determinism of orthodox Marxism. The notebooks also address [[Nationalism|Italian nationalism]], the [[French Revolution]], [[Civil society|civil society]], and [[Folklore|folklore]].

Venezuelan general and politician, president of [[Bolivia]] from 1825 to 1828. A close associate of [[Simón Bolívar]], he was a leading commander in the [[Spanish American wars of independence|wars of independence]] against the [[Spanish Empire]]. In 1822 his forces won the Battle of Pichincha and liberated [[Quito]], from which modern [[Ecuador]] would eventually emerge. In 1824 he defeated the Royalist army at Ayacucho, effectively securing the independence of Peru, and was named Grand Marshal of Ayacucho. After resigning the presidency in 1828, he commanded Colombian forces in the [[Gran Colombia]]–Peru War. He was [[Assassination|assassinated]] in Berruecos, Colombia, and the identity of the conspirators remains a subject of historical speculation.

Mexican general and politician, president of [[Mexico]] on multiple occasions between 1833 and 1855. He fought as a royalist officer in the [[Mexican War of Independence]] before joining the [[Insurgency|insurgency]] in 1821, and he frequently switched sides in conflicts between liberal and conservative factions. Elected as a liberal in 1833, he turned to the conservatives and overthrew his liberal vice president, Valentín Gómez Farías. He ruled in an ostentatious and [[Dictator|dictatorial]] style and used the military to dissolve Congress on several occasions. Under his rule Mexico lost Texas and then fought the [[Mexican–American War]]; historians have noted that he prolonged the conflict. In 1854 he ceded territory to the United States through the Gadsden Purchase. He died in [[Mexico City]].

Italian luthier who made [[String instrument|string instruments]] in Cremona, chiefly [[Violin|violins]], as well as [[Cello|cellos]], [[Viola|violas]], [[Guitar|guitars]], and [[Harp|harps]]. He is estimated to have produced 1,116 instruments, of which 960 were violins. Around 650 instruments survive, including 450 to 512 violins. His instruments are considered some of the finest ever made and are extremely valuable collector's items. The Latinized form of his surname, *Stradivarius*, and the colloquial *Strad* are often used for his instruments. He likely apprenticed with Nicola Amati, though this is debated, and unlike many of Amati's other students he did not repeatedly put Amati's name on his labels. The label of his oldest surviving violin is dated 1666.

Italian [[Baroque music|Baroque]] composer, virtuoso [[Violin|violinist]], and impresario. He consolidated the [[Concerto|concerto]] form, especially the solo concerto, and pioneered developments in orchestration and violin technique. He wrote many instrumental concertos, sacred choral works, and more than fifty operas, which were staged in [[Venice]], Mantua, and [[Vienna]]. His best-known work is *The Four Seasons*, a set of violin concertos. Many of his compositions were written for the all-female ensemble of the Ospedale della Pietà, [[Orphanage|a home for abandoned children]] in Venice. He began studying for the priesthood at 15 and was ordained at 25, but a health problem led to his dispensation from saying public Masses. After almost two centuries of decline, his reputation revived in the early 20th century, and many works once thought lost have been rediscovered.

Heavy strategic airlift cargo aircraft designed by the Antonov Design Bureau in the [[Soviet Union]]. Derived from the An-124 and built to carry Buran-class orbiters for the [[Soviet space program|Soviet space program]], it made its first flight on 21 December 1988. The name *Mriya* is Ukrainian for "dream." At a maximum takeoff weight of 640 tonnes, it was the heaviest aircraft ever built, and it carried oversized loads such as 130-ton generators and [[Wind turbine|wind turbine]] blades. Its only completed airframe was destroyed at Antonov Airport during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, and [[Volodymyr Zelenskyy]] announced plans to complete a second aircraft.

Port city in [[Flanders]], Belgium, and capital of Antwerp Province. The Port of Antwerp ranks second in Europe after [[Rotterdam]] and is among the top 20 ports globally. The city is the hub of the world's [[Diamond|diamond]] trade. Its [[Stock exchange|Stock Exchange]], built in 1531 and rebuilt in 1872, was the world's first purpose-built commodity exchange. Antwerp has long been an important city in the Low Countries, especially before and during the Spanish Fury of 1576 and the Dutch Revolt. The city hosted the Summer Olympics in 1920. Its population includes about 180 nationalities, and as of 2019 more than 50% of its population had a parent who was not a Belgian citizen at birth.

Ancient Egyptian god of funerary rites, protector of graves, and guide to the underworld in [[Ancient Egyptian religion|Egyptian religion]]. Usually depicted as a canine or as a man with a canine head, Anubis was shown in black, a color symbolizing regeneration and the soil of the [[Nile]]. He was protecting graves as early as the First Dynasty (c. 3100–c. 2890 BC) and was also an embalmer. By the Middle Kingdom (c. 2055–1650 BC) [[Osiris]] had replaced him as lord of the underworld, though Anubis continued to usher souls into the afterlife. He attended the [[Weighing scale|scale]] during the "Weighing of the Heart," which determined whether a soul could enter the realm of the dead. In early mythology he was portrayed as a son of [[Ra]]. In the Ptolemaic and Roman eras he was syncretized with [[Hermes]] as Hermanubis.

Body orifice at the exit end of the [[Gastrointestinal tract|digestive tract]], through which waste remaining after digestion is expelled. The name comes from [[Latin]] for "ring" or "circle." Expelled matter can include gas and semi-solid [[Feces|feces]], which may contain indigestible matter such as [[Bone|bones]], hair pellets, and seeds, as well as toxic substances and bile metabolites. Muscular sphincters control its passage, and failure to stop unwanted passages results in fecal incontinence. Amphibians, [[Reptile|reptiles]], and birds use a similar orifice, the [[Cloaca|cloaca]], for excreting wastes and for copulation and egg-laying. The anus appears to have evolved at least twice in multicellular animals, an important step that accompanied the bilaterian body plan and the coelom.

Indian actress known for films in Telugu and Tamil. Born Sweety Shetty in Mangalore, [[Karnataka]], she made her acting debut in the 2005 Telugu film *Super*. She won Filmfare Awards for Best Actress (Telugu) for *Arundhati* (2009) and *Vedam* (2010). Her portrayal of Princess Devasena in the *Baahubali* series (2015–17) received widespread acclaim. Media commentary often calls her the "Queen of South Indian cinema."

Egyptian politician and military officer, president of Egypt from 1970 to 1981. A member of the Free Officers movement, he served as vice president under [[Gamal Abdel Nasser]] on two occasions and succeeded him on Nasser's death. He departed from Nasserism by reinstituting a multi-party system and launching the *Infitah* economic policy. As president he led Egypt in the [[Yom Kippur War|October War]] of 1973 to regain the [[Sinai Peninsula]], which [[Israel]] had occupied since 1967. He then negotiated the Camp David Accords with [[Jimmy Carter]] and the Egypt–Israel peace treaty. Rejected by the [[Muslim Brotherhood]] and the left, the treaty was one factor leading to Egypt's suspension from the [[Arab League]] from 1979 to 1989. He was assassinated by militants during a military parade in Cairo.

Unpleasant [[Emotion|emotion]] of inner turmoil that includes dread over anticipated events. Unlike [[Fear|fear]], a response to a present threat, anxiety is the anticipation of a future one, and it is often accompanied by muscular tension, restlessness, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating. David Barlow defines it as "a future-oriented mood state in which one is not ready or prepared to attempt to cope with upcoming negative events." [[Evolutionary psychology|Evolutionary psychology]] interprets anxiety as a defense that helps organisms avoid threats, although such defenses can produce "false alarms." An [[Anxiety disorder]] is diagnosed when anxiety is excessive or persistent, typically for about 6 months. Anxiety can also occur within other conditions, including [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder]] and [[Post-traumatic stress disorder]].

Group of [[Mental disorder|mental disorders]] characterized by significant and uncontrollable anxiety and fear that impair social, occupational, and personal functioning. Types include generalized anxiety disorder, hypochondriasis, specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, separation anxiety disorder, [[Agoraphobia]], panic disorder, and selective mutism. A medical professional must rule out other medical illnesses and mental disorders before diagnosis. Lifetime prevalence of comorbid depression is 20–70% among people with social anxiety disorder, 50% with panic disorder, and 43% with generalized anxiety disorder. The 12-month prevalence of [[Alcohol (drug)|alcohol]] or [[Substance use disorder|substance use disorders]] among those with anxiety disorders is 16.5%. Worldwide, anxiety disorders are the second most common type of mental disorder after depressive disorders, with an estimated 5.8% of the global population currently affected.

Institutionalized system of racial segregation in [[South Africa]] from 1948 to 1994, also applied to South West Africa (now [[Namibia]]). The term is [[Afrikaans]] for "separateness." Racial discrimination dated to the [[Dutch East India Company]]'s trading post at the [[Cape of Good Hope]], established in 1652. Under apartheid, white citizens held the highest status. The Population Registration Act (1950) classified all South Africans by race, and the Immorality Amendment Act (1950) made most interracial marriages and sexual relationships illegal. Between 1960 and 1983, 3.5 million Black Africans were removed from their homes, mostly to confine the Black population to ten designated "tribal homelands," or bantustans. Internal resistance, including the [[African National Congress]], grew militant in the 1970s and 1980s, and the [[United Nations]] condemned the system. From 1987 to 1993 the National Party negotiated with the ANC, leading to non-racial elections in April 1994.

Self-contained housing unit occupying part of a [[Building|building]], called a flat in British English. Apartments range from public housing to owner-occupied condominiums and leaseholds, as well as units rented from private landlords. In the United States the word usually denotes a rental unit owned by the building owner. Apartment buildings contain three or more residences and are called tower blocks, high-rises, or blocks of flats in British English. Apartment buildings date to [[Ancient Rome]], where *insulae* housed lower-class tenants. High-rise apartments became possible with the invention of the [[Elevator|elevator]] and cheaper building materials. A building with fifty or more stories is generally considered a [[Skyscraper|skyscraper]].

Tailless [[Primate|primate]] of the superfamily Hominoidea. Apes are more closely related to [[Old World monkey|Old World monkeys]] than to New World monkeys, and they lack tails due to a mutation of the TBXT gene. Apes are native to [[Sub-Saharan Africa]] and [[Southeast Asia]], though they were once more widespread in Africa, Asia, and Europe. The lesser apes, or [[Gibbon|gibbons]], include 20 species, all native to Asia. The great apes include three extant species of orangutans, two of gorillas, two of chimpanzees, and [[Human|humans]]. Except for gorillas and humans, apes are agile tree climbers. All extant non-human hominoids are rare and threatened with [[Extinction]], mainly from habitat loss, and the great apes of Africa also face the [[Ebola]] virus.

[[Mountain range|Mountain range]] of parallel chains extending c. 1,200 km (750 mi) the length of peninsular [[Italy]]. In the northwest the range joins the Ligurian Alps, and in the southwest it ends at Reggio di Calabria. Since 2000 Italy's Environment Ministry has defined the Apennines System to include the mountains of northern [[Sicily]], a total of 1,500 kilometres (930 mi). The Apennines preserve some of the best-preserved forests and montane [[Grassland|grasslands]] in Europe, protected by national parks, and they are among the few places where large predators such as the Italian wolf and the Marsican brown bear still exist, which are now extinct in the rest of [[Central Europe]]. The highest peak, Corno Grande, is partly covered by the Calderone [[Glacier|glacier]], the only glacier in the Apennines. The eastern slopes fall steeply to the [[Adriatic Sea]].

Predator at the top of a food chain, with few or no natural predators. Apex predators occupy the highest trophic levels, and the group dates at least to the [[Cambrian]] period. They affect prey populations and other predators, and their removal can trigger trophic cascades: the hunting of [[Sperm whale|sperm whales]] caused an increase in the population of large squid. [[Human|Humans]] are themselves apex predators, and they interact with others such as wolves through hunting and with the Iberian [[Lynx]] through rewilding.

Impairment of the ability to comprehend or formulate [[Language|language]], caused by dysfunction in specific brain regions. [[Stroke]] and head trauma are the major causes, and aphasia due to stroke is estimated at 0.1–0.4% in developed countries. It can also result from [[Brain tumor|brain tumors]], [[Epilepsy]], multiple sclerosis, or neurodegenerative diseases such as [[Dementia]]. Intelligence is unaffected, but speech, reading, writing, and [[Sign language|sign language]] may all be impaired. Anomia, difficulty finding the correct word, is a prevalent deficit in all aphasias. Formulaic expressions are often preserved, so a person who cannot ask a loved one about their birthday may still sing "Happy Birthday."

British musician, composer, and DJ, known professionally as Aphex Twin and active in [[Electronic music|electronic music]] since 1988. Raised in [[Cornwall]], he began DJing at free parties and clubs in the South West in the late 1980s. His debut EP, *Analogue Bubblebath* (1991), and the album *Selected Ambient Works 85–92* (1992) brought him an early following. His work draws on techno, ambient, acid, and jungle and is closely associated with intelligent dance music. The singles "Come to Daddy" (1997) and "Windowlicker" (1999), with music videos by Chris Cunningham, brought him international attention. *Syro* (2014) won the Grammy Award for Best Dance/Electronic Album.
